::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Combinatorics , function](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5128012/combinatorics-function), asked by [Rupam Das](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1746515/rupam-das) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2026-03-09; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Consider all functions $f:\{1,2,3,4\}\to\{1,2,3,4\}$ which are one--one, onto and satisfy the following property:
> $f(k)$ is odd if and only if $f(k + 1)$ is even, for $k = 1, 2, 3.$
> Find the number of such functions.
>
> {My Doubt:} Since the function is one--one and onto, it must be a permutation of $\{1,2,3,4\}$. The given condition implies that the parity alternates. Hence the only possible pattern is $(\text{odd},\text{even},\text{odd},\text{even})$ because any other pattern would violate the condition. There are two odd numbers $\{1,3\}$ and two even numbers $\{2,4\}$. The odd numbers can be arranged among themselves in $2!=2$ ways, and the even numbers can also be arranged in $2!=2$ ways. Thus the total number of such functions should be $2\times2=4$. However, the given answer is $2$. Am I correct or wrong?
:::

I agree with you that the parities alternate. Since there are only two odd numbers and two even numbers in $\{1,2,3,4\}$, the entire bijection is determined by $f(1)$ and $f(2)$. If $f(1)$ is odd, then $f(2)$ is even, and there are $2 \times 2 = 4$ bijections. They are:
$$(1,2,3,4),\ (1,4,3,2),\ (3,2,1,4),\ (3,4,1,2)$$

This is already more than the expected answer, so either the expected answer is incorrect, or the instructions have been misunderstood.

Several commenters and I interpreted the conditions “$f(k)$ is odd if and only if $f(k + 1)$ is even, for $k = 1, 2, 3$” to mean “$f(1)$ and $f(2)$” have opposite parity, $f(2)$ and $f(3)$ have opposite parity, and $f(3)$ and $f(4)$ have opposite parity.” Since $k=4$ is not included in the list, there doesn't seem to be any problem with $5$ not being in the domain of these bijections.

This means that any of the four numbers $\{1,2,3,4\}$ is eligible to be $f(1)$, while $f(2)$ must be one of the two numbers opposite in parity to $f(1)$. This yields four more bijections:
$$(2,1,3,4),\ (2,3,1,4),\ (4,1,3,2),\ (4,3,2,1)$$

So I get eight in total.
